finding: §3 twice cites a table that this round deleted. Line 186 reads "a fence built from the three shapes in the table above would not", and §7 row 13b's mutant reads "build the fence from the three shapes in §3's table, which do not reach this input". §3 contains no table at all — the only tables in the file are at lines 43, 88, 121 and 333, none of them in §3, and the rejected-rules table was cut this round. Both references are load-bearing rather than decorative: row 13b's mutant is defined entirely as "the three shapes in §3's table", so with the table gone the row names no mutant an implementer can build, and §3's own argument for the change rule rests on a comparison against a set the reader cannot see.
suggestion: Either restore the three shapes inline in §3 (field-scoped / value-scoped / literal-transition, one clause each) and keep the two references, or rewrite both sentences to name the three narrower rules §3 already spells out in prose at lines 166-170 and drop the words "the table".

finding: The header epigraph names §6's own content as the example of what must not be in this file. It says a repository survey — "line-number citations, counted enumerations, which of eleven assertions survive" — belongs in task acceptance, not here. §6 item 1 is exactly that survey: "Two of the eleven `assert.`/`require.` call sites in `TestAuditGate_NoEscapeHatchFromTheGate` (`internal/cli/audit_signal_test.go`); the other nine stand — nine under that counting rule, which includes two `require.True(t, ok)` decode checks, and the rule is stated because without it the number is 7." §7 row 18 then pins the count of eleven as a test assertion, so the release both forbids the enumeration and normatively requires it. §6's own preamble makes the collision sharper: it says "the release owes the derivation instead of the count" and "the count has been one, two, three and five, and each number was falsified by the next round" — and then item 1 ships a new count of eleven with a bespoke counting rule to defend it. §6.5's measurements are different and the epigraph permits them ("measurements that justify a decision stay"); the eleven call sites justify no decision, they only describe a tree.
suggestion: Delete the call-site arithmetic from item 1 and state the decision instead — the guard must assert that `audit_converge_on` IS a known workflow field, and every other assertion in that test is unchanged. Move the count and its counting rule into the task's acceptance, where it is re-derived from the tree, and re-word §7 row 18 to assert the reversal and the absence of deletions without naming a total.

finding: Row 11's named mutant cannot fail row 11, and the fact it cites is false. The mutant is "count the streak as a total rather than a trailing run — v0.35.0 has three clean-under-`blocking` rounds before round 3, so a total reaches 2 one round early". Measured over spec/.tp-review/0.35.0/audit-round-*.ndjson, the clean-under-`blocking` rounds are 2,3,5,6,7,8,9 and the unclean ones are 1 (2 error) and 4 (1 error) — so exactly ONE clean round precedes round 3, not three. Because round 1 is unclean and rounds 2 and 3 are both clean, a total and a trailing run reach 2 at the same round. Replaying all eight cells row 11 asserts under both rules gives identical answers: blocking 3 / all 9 at audit_clean_rounds 2 and blocking 2 / all 8 at 1 for v0.35.0, and blocking 3 / all never at 2 and blocking 2 / all never at 1 for v0.36.0. A row whose mutant leaves every asserted number unchanged pins the trailing-run rule not at all, which §7's own preamble forbids.
suggestion: Replace the mutant with one the corpus can distinguish — the natural one is a streak that does not reset on an unclean round mid-history, which v0.35.0's round 4 (`error`) does discriminate for any assertion covering rounds 5-7 — or add a synthetic fixture with a clean/unclean/clean prefix and assert on it. Delete the "three clean rounds before round 3" claim; it is false on the data the row replays.

finding: §6.5 misstates the shipped caveat it exists to price, in both direction and extent. It says the object's "third message form counts rows carrying no `role` as `unattributed_open` and warns that the spec-coverage streak may be UNDERSTATED". The shipped strings in `engine.divergenceMessage` say the opposite: "none attributed to a role (possibly spec-coverage's)" and "(including %d with no role, which may be spec-coverage's)". The hazard they name is that an open row belongs to spec-coverage while `auditRoundOpenByRole` skips roleless rows, so spec-coverage is reported clean when it is not — the streak is OVERSTATED, not understated. The direction is the whole point: an understated streak delays a release, an overstated one ships over an unmeasured conformance failure, and §6.5 tells the operator they are accepting the harmless one. Extent is wrong too: two of the three message forms carry the caveat, not the third alone — the `unattributedOpen == otherRolesOpen` form carries it as well, and that is the form §6.5's own corpus produces (spec/.tp-review/0.23.0/audit-round-1.ndjson has one non-PASS row and it is roleless).
suggestion: Rewrite the sentence to say the caveat warns the spec-coverage streak may be OVERSTATED because a roleless open row may be spec-coverage's, and that two of the three message forms carry it. Then re-check the paragraph's conclusion: the price the release accepts is losing a warning about a possibly-false clean conformance streak, which is a larger claim than "understated" makes it look.

finding: The fence is defined over "the resolved value", but resolution in tp is per task file — `engine.ResolveWorkflow(specPath, flagFile)` needs a spec path to reach the task-override layer, and this repository holds one `<base>.tasks.json` per version. "The resolved value" is therefore not single-valued for the two sinks that write below the task layer. §3's must-pass example — "a `--project` write of `blocking` beneath a task override of `all` changes nothing an audit will read and must pass" — is stated for a repo with exactly one task file. With two (T1 overriding `all`, T2 carrying no override) the same `tp set --project audit_converge_on=blocking` changes what T2 resolves and not what T1 resolves, and §3 gives no rule for which comparison the fence makes: any-spec, all-specs, or the active pointer's. `tp set --project` takes no spec argument, so the implementer must invent the enumeration. §7 row 13 pins only the single-task-file shape, so every choice passes the suite.
suggestion: State the quantifier in §3: the fence refuses when the write changes the resolved value to `blocking` for ANY task file discovered under the repository (plus the no-task-file resolution, which the project layer also governs), and say explicitly that `tp set --project` enumerates task files to evaluate it. Add a §7 row with two task files that differ in their override, asserting the refusal fires on the one that changes and pins which population is compared.

finding: §3's claim that `tp config --extract` is "resolution-preserving by construction" holds only for the task files present at the moment of the hoist, and the fence has no clause for what happens afterwards. `hoistedFields`/`computeCommonPolicy` hoist a field only when every task file already carries the same value and then strip it from those files — so if every task file carries `blocking`, the extract writes `blocking` into `.tp/config.json`. Every task file created after that (by `tp init`, or by a decompose unit) carries no override and now resolves `blocking` from the project layer, in a cycle for which no human made the decision §3 says is human-only. The composite path is unfenced end to end: `tp config --extract` (no unattended fence, only a clean-tree gate) followed by any later `tp import`, whose change rule compares resolved-before `blocking` against resolved-after `blocking` and passes. §3's sentence "the sink that uncovers is `tp import`" is an exhaustive claim over the write paths and this falsifies it — `--extract` is a sink that uncovers on every future task file, not on the ones it hoisted from.
suggestion: Either fence `tp config --extract` under `TP_UNATTENDED=1` when the hoisted value is `blocking`, or exclude `audit_converge_on` from `hoistedFields` and say why (which contradicts §7 row 4, so pick one). If it is kept hoistable, replace "resolution-preserving by construction" with the accurate scope — preserving for the task files it hoisted from, and prospectively binding for every task file created afterwards — and add a §7 row for the extract-then-init sequence.

finding: §4's premise for what is missing is false, and it makes three different populations share one name across the release. §4 says "The *count* of them is already emitted — `role_streaks[].open` is severity-blind and unconditional on both `--status` and `--record`". `role_streaks[].open` is a PER-ROLE count, not the round's total, and `engine.auditRoundOpenByRole` skips every row carrying no role — the exact 20 rows §6.5 counts and prices. So on a round holding roleless open rows the sum of `role_streaks[].open` is strictly less than the round's non-PASS count, and the count §4 says is "already emitted" is not. Meanwhile `--record` already emits the round total as `findings`, which §4 does not mention, and §2 defines the next_action count as a third phrasing, "the non-`PASS` rows of the latest recorded round". Three populations, one word, in one release — and §6.5 is the section that proves they differ.
suggestion: Correct §4's premise: on `--record` the round total is already emitted as `findings`; on `--status` it is recoverable from the stored round; `role_streaks[].open` is per-role and roleless-blind and is not that count. Then state once, in §2, which population `next_action`'s count and §4's buckets are over — the latest round's non-PASS rows including roleless ones — and say that this deliberately differs from the sum of `role_streaks[].open`.

finding: §1 says "Three deliverables" and then spends the ordinal "fourth" on the item that was CUT ("A fourth, a spec-hash reset ... is now `spec/0.46.0.md` §8.4"), while §6 opens with "This is work, not a Non-Goal" and receives five of §7's twenty-six test rows (18-22) — more rows than §4 and §3 combined. A decomposer sizing the release from §1, which is what §1 is for, sees three deliverables plus one deferral and misses a fifth of the test surface: a const rewrite, a doc-comment rewrite, two documentation rewrites, a guard-test reversal, a new guard assertion over REFERENCE.md, and a corpus-wide sweep across `skills/`, `README.md`, `internal/engine/` and `internal/cli/`. §6 explicitly says it is stated as its own section "because a decomposer reads the Non-Goals to learn what *not* to build" — the same reader reads §1 to learn what TO build, and §1 does not carry it.
suggestion: Make it four deliverables and give §6's sweep its own numbered entry in §1, naming the four surfaces it crosses. Refer to the cut spec-hash reset without an ordinal ("a fifth item, cut" or simply "a deferred item") so the word "fourth" is not held by something that does not ship.

finding: §7's closing paragraph presents its list of untested surfaces as complete ("Not tested here, named so the absence is deliberate") and names only `role_streaks[].open`, `consecutive_clean` and `spec_coverage_clean_rounds`. At least three decisions the spec makes normatively are pinned by no row and appear in no absence list. (1) §2's next_action table decides TWO branches — "clean, not yet converged" gets "run the next audit round, **and name the accepted count**" — and row 10 tests only the converged branch, so the branch tp will actually spend most rounds in is unpinned, and §2 says both "are decided here rather than left to an implementer". (2) §2.1 states a deliverable — "`skills/tp/SKILL.md` carries the one-line command that derives it, next to the field's documentation" — with no row. (3) §6's sweep, which §6 calls the deliverable in place of the count, has no row; §6 says the task's acceptance runs it, but §7 never says so, so the reader of §7 alone concludes it is untested by oversight.
suggestion: Add a row for the not-yet-converged branch (the same fixture as row 10, one round earlier, asserting the count appears in the non-converged string too). Add a row or an explicit acceptance pointer for §2.1's SKILL.md command. Add one sentence to §7's closing paragraph saying the §6 sweep is verified in task acceptance rather than by a test, so the absence reads as deliberate.

finding: §4 states its problem on one command and ships its answer on another. The motivating sentence is "without it an agent reading `clean: true` cannot see what was suppressed" — but `clean` is emitted only by `tp audit --record` and (per round, inside `audit_rounds`) by `--status`; `tp audit --merge` never emits `clean` at all, and §4 is explicit that it cannot even resolve the policy. So the agent who reads `clean: true` on the gating sink still cannot see the breakdown, and the agent who can see the breakdown is looking at a payload with no verdict in it. §5 item 4 defers the record/status surface, which is a legitimate scope decision, but §4 then describes the merge-only breakdown as "the audit-side visibility this release ships" without saying that the visibility lands on a different command from the decision it is meant to inform — and `--merge` is optional in the audit loop as CLAUDE.md's Workflow D writes it.
suggestion: Rewrite §4's opening to name the actual reader: an agent running `--merge` immediately before `--record`, who sees the breakdown one command earlier than the verdict. Say plainly that a cycle which records without merging gets no breakdown, and that closing that gap is §5 item 4's deferral rather than something this release delivers.

finding: After this release the two twin fields carry the same two literals with opposite defaults, and no section says so. `engine.ResolveWorkflowLayers` defaults `review_converge_on` to `blocking` (configresolve.go: `ReviewConvergeOn: ReviewConvergeOnBlocking`), so review already ships with advisory findings not counted; §2 makes `audit_converge_on` default to `all`, the strict value. §1's opening sentence depends on the review default without naming it ("`review_converge_on` lets the review loop stop counting advisory findings" is true out of the box only because its default is `blocking`), and §2.1 argues the audit default at length without ever noting that the twin ships the opposite one. The consequence is on the reader of a config file: `review_converge_on` unset and `audit_converge_on` unset mean opposite policies, and §3's fence exists for one of them and not the other. §7 row 1 and row 2 assert structural parity (same precedence, same literals, same hint) which makes the divergence harder to notice, not easier.
suggestion: Add one sentence to §2.1 stating the asymmetry and why it is deliberate: review's relaxed value is its default because a review finding is advice, while an audit finding is a conformance claim, so audit opts in. Then check that §6's sweep clause (d) covers any shipped sentence that describes the two fields as behaving alike.

finding: The release refuses one disposition word and then adopts a stronger one in its own normative output. §2 says "*Surviving* is deliberately not the word: it would imply a disposition that removes a row from the count, which §5 declines to create" — and then §2's own next_action table says "when the round holds ACCEPTED rows" and "name the ACCEPTED count", §7 row 10 asserts "the count of accepted rows", and §7 row 19 puts the word into a SHIPPED constant: `engine.DivergenceHint` and SKILL.md are to say convergence counts every non-PASS row "the resolved policy does not ACCEPT". "Accepted" implies a per-row disposition at least as strongly as "surviving" does, and §5 item 2 says no such mechanism ships. The version in the shipped constant is the costly one: an agent reading "the resolved policy does not accept" will look for the accept/reject step and find none.
suggestion: Pick one vocabulary and use it in the table, in row 10, and in the replacement sentences. "Non-blocking" or "advisory" describes the population without implying an act: the table row becomes "name the count of non-blocking open rows" and row 19's sentence becomes "counts every non-PASS row of a blocking severity under the resolved policy" — but check that phrasing against row 19's own second mutant, which rules out "whose severity is blocking" for the `all` case, so the sentence needs the policy named rather than the severity.

finding: §2 puts one JSON key name on both sides of its own boundary without saying so. It lists `engine.ConsecutiveClean` among the things that change with the stored flag, and three lines earlier says "`role_streaks[].open`, its `consecutive_clean` and `spec_coverage_clean_rounds` stay severity-blind". Both are real and both are emitted in the same payload: `audit_record.go` writes a top-level `"consecutive_clean": engine.ConsecutiveClean(...)` derived from the stored `clean` flags, while `engine.RoleStreak` serializes a per-role `"consecutive_clean"` computed from `auditRoundOpenByRole`, which is severity-blind by construction. Under `blocking` these two same-named numbers diverge on exactly the rounds the release is for, and nothing in §7 pins that divergence, so an implementer who routes the per-role streak through the stored flag for consistency breaks nothing the suite can see.
suggestion: Say it in §2: the top-level `consecutive_clean` follows the stamped `clean` and therefore the policy, while `role_streaks[].consecutive_clean` and `spec_coverage_clean_rounds` stay row-derived and severity-blind, so the two same-named keys can disagree under `blocking`. Add a §7 row asserting a payload where they do.

finding: §3 tells the implementer to copy the very function §7 forbids reusing, and the spec never separates the two. §3 says "The string-shaped fence tp already runs — placed before the type dispatch — is what to copy"; the only string-shaped unattended fence tp runs is `engine.FencedCommandField` + `refuseUnattendedCommandField`, and it is indeed placed before the type dispatch (`set.go` checks it before `editableWorkflowFields`/`floatWorkflowFields`). §7 row 14's mutant is "reuse `refuseUnattendedCommandField`, which interpolates this field's name and so passes any assertion phrased as 'the message names the field'". "Copy the placement" and "do not reuse the message" is a coherent instruction, but neither §3 nor row 14 says which half is which, so an implementer reading §3 first has been told to copy exactly what row 14 will fail them for.
suggestion: Name the function in §3 and split the instruction: copy `FencedCommandField`'s call-site POSITION (before the type dispatch, at every write sink) and write a new refusal message; do not call `refuseUnattendedCommandField`. One clause removes the ambiguity and makes row 14's mutant read as a consequence rather than a contradiction.

finding: Five citations point at subsections §6 does not have. §2 cites "§6.5", and §7 rows 18-22 cite "§6.1", "§6.2-3", "§6.4" and "§6.5" twice — but §6 is a flat section whose only structure is a numbered list, so nothing in the document is addressable as §6.1. The ambiguity is not merely cosmetic at §6.5: §2 uses it for the unnumbered paragraph "What suppression costs" (line 306), §7 row 21 uses it for list item 5 (`ComputeAuditDivergence`'s doc comment), and row 22 uses it for the paragraph again — three referents, one anchor, in a release whose review findings dedup on the section anchor. This also survived the renumber that turned §6a into §6 and §6 into §5, so the anchors were rewritten without the sections they name being created.
suggestion: Promote §6's five items to `### 6.1` ... `### 6.5` headings, and give "What suppression costs" its own `### 6.6` so §2's citation and row 22's resolve to different sections. Alternatively drop the sub-numbers and cite "§6 item 5", which the `broken-cross-ref` lint already understands.

finding: Bare `spec/0.46.0.md` §8 is given three different subjects inside this file, and §5 item 1 denies one of them. §5 item 1 says §8 is the `--check` divergence and states flatly "That is role scoping, not severity scoping, and severity parity does not close it". §6.5 then says "Making `divergence` severity-aware is `spec/0.46.0.md` §8's subject" — a severity subject — and §7's closing paragraph gives §8 a third one, "`role_streaks[].open`, `consecutive_clean` and `spec_coverage_clean_rounds` stay severity-blind ...; `spec/0.46.0.md` §8 owns changing that". §7 row 22's mutant adds a fourth use ("which is `spec/0.46.0.md` §8's decision to make"). Meanwhile §5 items 2-4 and §1 cite the precise subsections §8.1-§8.4. A reader following the bare §8 pointer from §6.5 lands on the section §5 has just told them is about something else.
suggestion: Give each bare §8 citation its subsection, as §5 items 2-4 already do. If severity-aware divergence and severity-aware streaks have no subsection in `spec/0.46.0.md` yet, say so in the pointer ("§8, which does not yet carry this") rather than implying it is already owned, and re-check that §5 item 1's denial and §6.5's assignment are not both describing §8's top level.

finding: §2.1 says the operator accepts the trade "with the numbers in front of them", and three paragraphs earlier says the decision is made at "the moment an operator has none of the evidence this table offers". The evidence the release does supply — a one-line command deriving the PREVIOUS cycle's severity mix from its `audit-round-*.ndjson` — does not measure the risk §2.1 says is being accepted. That risk is whether an `error` row appears in a round AFTER the point `blocking` would have halted, which §2.1 itself makes the decisive fact ("`blocking` would have shipped over an `error` row in 2 of 2 measured cycles"). A severity histogram over a whole past cycle cannot answer it: v0.35.0's mix is 3 error / 22 warning / 17 info whether the errors sat in round 1 or round 4, and it was round 4 that decided the default. The release therefore hands the operator a statistic that reads reassuring in exactly the cycles that argue against the setting.
suggestion: Make the derived number the one that decides: for each past cycle, the round `blocking` would have halted at and whether any later round carried an `error`. That is derivable from the same files by the same command shape, and it is the number §2.1 uses for its own conclusion. Then "with the numbers in front of them" is true.

finding: §6 says "**Items 1, 2 and 3 are three coordinated edits, not one**" and then supports it with an argument that covers only items 2 and 3: "The guard asserts the sentence twice and independently — once as the test-local literal against `SKILL.md`, once as the constant against `REFERENCE.md` — so editing `engine.DivergenceHint` alone leaves `SKILL.md` green." Item 1 is a different guard in a different file (`TestAuditGate_NoEscapeHatchFromTheGate` in `internal/cli/audit_signal_test.go`) asserting a different thing (that the field is an unknown workflow field), and nothing in the paragraph explains what it is coordinated WITH or why it must land in the same change. The grouping decides task granularity, so a decomposer either writes one task for three unrelated edits or splits it and loses the coordination the sentence was written to protect.
suggestion: Either drop item 1 from the sentence and make it "Items 2 and 3 are two coordinated edits", or state item 1's coupling explicitly — it must land with §2's implementation, since the guard fails the moment the field becomes known, and it is coordinated with the field's existence rather than with the two sentences.

finding: §2 presents a quotation of the review twin's design rationale that does not appear in the source. It reads: the review twin recomputes live, by design, "so a later `--resolve` or converge-on switch re-evaluates it without re-recording". The comment on `engine.ReviewRoundClean` says "switching review_converge_on or resolving a finding wontfix after the round was recorded both re-evaluate the round's cleanliness without re-recording". The paraphrase is faithful in substance but is inside quotation marks, and it narrows the source in one respect the release cares about — the source names resolving a finding *wontfix*, not `--resolve` generally, and §5 item 2 turns on exactly whether a disposition exists.
suggestion: Either quote the comment verbatim or drop the quotation marks and paraphrase in the spec's own voice. If the quote is kept, keep "wontfix" in it, since §5 item 2's deferral is about that disposition.

finding: §7's rows run 12, 13, 13b, 13d, 13c — the `d` suffix precedes the `c`. Every other suffixed pair in the table (9 / 9b) is in order. The table is the artifact tasks are decomposed from and rows are cited by number elsewhere in the file (§3 cites "rows 13 and 13b"), so an out-of-order pair is a small but real source of mis-citation.
suggestion: Swap the two rows so the sequence reads 13, 13b, 13c, 13d, or renumber the four fence rows 12, 13, 14, 15 and shift the rest — the suffix letters no longer carry information now that the section they were inserted into has been rewritten.
